entries.title: What SMPL is
entries.answer: SMPL.ai is a Financial Intelligence platform built specifically for SaaS companies. It works alongside the accounting system, CRM, HR, and billing platforms a finance team already uses, and automates the work of collecting, reconciling, analyzing, and explaining financial data — delivering executive-ready reporting in minutes after close, with the evidence behind every number.
entries.source: Executive Summary, 'What SMPL.ai is'

entries.title: Not a dashboard / BI tool
topics: how is this different from BI
isn't this just a BI tool
keywords: how is this different from bi
isn't this just a bi tool
entries.answer: It isn't a dashboard and it isn't a system of record. It's the decision-support layer that sits above the systems of record — the layer every SaaS finance team currently rebuilds by hand in spreadsheets every month. A BI tool lets you drill from a summary toward more granular numbers within one system; our lineage runs all the way to the original source record, whichever system it came from.
entries.source: Investor Overview + Technical Whitepaper, canonical data model

entries.title: What makes SMPL different
entries.answer: Three things, by design and not as features bolted on: consistent results — the same inputs always produce the same outputs; transparent by design — every conclusion traces to underlying evidence and uncertainty is flagged, not hidden; and institutional knowledge — we preserve how your organization defines and measures its business and reproduce any report exactly as it was originally delivered.
entries.source: Executive Summary, 'What makes SMPL.ai different'

entries.title: Adapts to your process
topics: do we have to change our process
how do you handle our ARR definition
keywords: do we have to change our process
how do you handle our arr definition
entries.answer: SMPL adapts to your finance organization instead of asking you to adapt to the software. You keep your definition of ARR, your forecasting methodology, and the board metrics your leadership already understands — the platform learns them once and automates them. Methodology is configuration the engine executes, not hardcoded logic, so the engine is the same for every customer but your configuration is yours.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Financial Intelligence Engine

entries.title: Deterministic calculations
entries.answer: Every calculation is deterministic: given the same inputs and methodology configuration, the engine returns the identical output on every run. The mechanism is versioning, not caching — each calculation runs against a specific timestamped snapshot. A report generated in March, reproduced today, reads exactly as it did in March, even if the underlying data was later corrected. Both the old and new views are correct; they answer 'what did we know then' versus 'what do we know now.'
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Deterministic Calculations

entries.title: Evidence and explainability
topics: can you back up the numbers
keywords: can you back up the numbers
entries.answer: Every number traces to the specific source records that produced it — an invoice, an opportunity, a GL entry — not just an intermediate total. Explanations are generated the same way: a statement like 'expansion ARR beat forecast by $420K, driven by three enterprise upsells that closed early' comes from those three actual opportunity records, not a template. If the data doesn't support a specific explanation, the platform says so rather than inventing a plausible-sounding one.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Explainability and Evidence

entries.title: Confidence signals on numbers
entries.answer: Every number and explanation carries an explicit confidence signal. A value from complete, well-structured data reads high-confidence; a value derived by inference — say, ARR estimated from invoice history rather than an explicit contract record — reads visibly lower, with a note on what would resolve it. Confidence is never collapsed into false certainty in either direction.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Explainability and Evidence

entries.title: Period close governance
entries.answer: Each reporting period moves through an explicit close workflow. Once a period is finalized, corrections do not rewrite history — they are recorded as new dated entries that supersede the previous ones. That way you can always answer what the numbers were when leadership made a decision, versus what they are after a correction.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Governance

entries.title: Period close governance (internal deep)
entries.answer: Each reporting period moves through an explicit workflow: load, validate, lock, freeze, report. Once frozen, a period doesn't reopen — a correction is recorded as a new dated entry linked to the one it supersedes, producing a new snapshot going forward while the original stays intact. That's what makes 'what did we know, and when did we know it' an answerable question rather than an aspiration.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Governance (internal)

entries.title: vs Cube
topics: how do you compare to Cube
keywords: how do you compare to cube
entries.answer: Cube serves a similar buyer, and its AI messaging now sounds like ours on paper. The difference is architectural: Cube's core product is a bi-directional Excel and Sheets sync — the finance team still builds and maintains the model in spreadsheets, and Cube's AI makes that faster. That architecture can't guarantee deterministic calculations or board decks that reproduce exactly after a restatement. Cube makes a team faster at the work; we do the work and hand the team a defensible result to review.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Competitive Landscape

entries.title: vs QuickBooks / incumbents
entries.answer: Incumbent accounting platforms are shipping AI variance analysis and commentary, and they'll keep closing surface-level feature gaps. Our durable advantage isn't a feature checklist — it's a data architecture built natively for SaaS metrics like ARR waterfalls, NRR and GRR, and quota ramp curves, with determinism and evidence attached by design, not general-ledger AI bolted on after the fact.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Competitive Landscape

entries.title: vs Rillet
topics: how do you compare to Rillet
keywords: how do you compare to rillet
entries.answer: Rillet isn't a competitor — it replaces the system of record, while we supply the intelligence layer that sits above it and any other general ledger. We actually see a natural, complementary partnership opportunity there and are pursuing it.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Competitive Landscape

entries.title: Target market / ICP
entries.answer: High-growth SaaS companies in roughly the $5 million to $50 million ARR range — the band where finance complexity first outpaces finance headcount, where companies first build a real FP&A function and first outgrow QuickBooks and spreadsheets at the same time. There are more than 27,000 SaaS companies in the US alone.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Market opportunity

entries.title: Market growth
entries.answer: Estimates of the FP&A software market range from roughly $5 to $9 billion today, and nearly all of them agree on the direction: double-digit growth driven by the shift from spreadsheet-based planning to AI-native platforms. MGI Research puts cloud FP&A at nearly $8.5 billion in 2026, growing 28 percent year over year.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Market opportunity

entries.title: Business impact / ROI
topics: how much time do you save
keywords: how much time do you save
entries.answer: Four things. Speed — reporting that takes weeks after close is done in minutes once data is loaded. Effort — a single ARR reporting package can consume 40 to 80 hours of finance time today, and we automate most of it. Confidence — every deliverable ships with the data behind it, reviewed before it's shared. Alignment — finance, leadership, and the board work from one trusted view instead of reconciling spreadsheets.
entries.source: Executive Summary, Business impact

entries.title: Business model
entries.answer: A subscription platform sold directly to finance leadership, with a land-and-expand motion: customers start with core financial reporting and close automation, then expand into GTM efficiency, workforce modeling, and scenario planning as trust builds. Go-to-market runs through direct outreach to CFOs and VPs of Finance, plus partnerships with modern accounting platforms and advisory firms that reach the same buyer warmer than cold outbound.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Business model

entries.title: Where we are / traction
entries.answer: Platform design is complete — every data connection, calculation, and control is fully specified — and we can demonstrate it today on realistic SaaS data. We're not yet live with paying customers, which is exactly why we're bringing in a small number of design partners first, to validate against real data and shape the roadmap ahead of general availability.
entries.source: Executive Summary / Investor Overview, Where we are

entries.title: Implementation timeline
entries.answer: Implementation is designed to run about four to six weeks per customer. We integrate with the systems you already use — accounting/GL, CRM, HRIS, and billing — and deliver a secure browser-based application: nothing to install and no infrastructure for your team to manage.

entries.title: How customers can trust our security
topics: how do we trust your security
why should we trust you with our data
keywords: how do we trust your security
why should we trust you with our data
entries.answer: Trust starts with architecture, not a slogan. SMPL is a browser-based SaaS that reads and reconciles your finance systems — it does not post back to your GL or ERP. Data is encrypted in transit with TLS and at rest in managed Postgres. Tenants are isolated by organization ID on every warehouse path. Access today is invite-based magic-link login with role-based views, from finance drill-down to summary board views. AI keys stay on the API; narrative is drafted from engine outputs, not invented ledger numbers. We are pursuing SOC 2 Type I with Security, Availability, and Confidentiality in scope — we do not claim a completed SOC 2 report today. Happy to walk IT through the architecture diagram, DPA, and questionnaire answers.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram + SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 + Technical Whitepaper

entries.title: Encryption in transit and at rest
entries.answer: Yes. Traffic to the application and API is protected with HTTPS/TLS in transit. Customer warehouse data is stored in managed Postgres with encryption at rest provided by the database platform. That is the baseline we document for IT questionnaires and security reviews.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Security Posture; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2

entries.title: Multi-tenant isolation
topics: can another customer see our data
keywords: can another customer see our data
entries.answer: The warehouse and API are multi-tenant by design. Customer data is scoped by organization ID, and API queries require that tenant context — Org A cannot read Org B's warehouse. That isolation model is what we document for security reviews and SOC 2 readiness evidence.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; Architecture Master, Multi-tenancy; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2

entries.title: No GL / ERP write-back
topics: do you write back to our ERP
do you post to the GL
keywords: do you post to the gl
do you write back to our erp
entries.answer: No. SMPL reads and reconciles source systems — accounting/GL, CRM, billing, HRIS — and does not post journals or write back into your ERP or general ledger. Your systems of record stay systems of record; we are the intelligence layer above them.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; Architecture Master; GO_LIVE_POC_DIRECT_DATA_ACCESS

entries.title: Hosting and deployment model
entries.answer: SMPL is a secure browser-based SaaS application — no customer-installed client and no infrastructure for your team to manage. End users access dashboards and exports through a modern browser. The standard deployment separates the web app, API services, and multi-tenant Postgres warehouse, with production and sandbox environments. We can share the IT technical diagram under NDA for architecture review.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; Technical Whitepaper, Delivery

entries.title: Named subprocessors (sales-internal)
entries.answer: Sales-internal named stack (confirm before customer-facing disclosure packs): frontend on Vercel (Next.js), API on Railway (FastAPI), warehouse/auth data on Neon Postgres, magic-link email via Resend, AI narrative via Anthropic Claude with OpenAI as fallback, billing via Stripe. Prefer the abstracted architecture language externally unless the prospect has the current subprocessors list / DPA exhibit. Update this list whenever vendors change.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 §7–8

entries.title: Where customer data is stored
entries.answer: Customer financial warehouse data lives in our managed multi-tenant Postgres database, accessed only through the application and API with tenant scoping. The web app and API run on managed cloud hosts — not on customer laptops or on-prem servers. Exact region and the named vendor list are covered in the subprocessors / DPA materials we share for IT review; we do not invent residency guarantees that are not in those documents.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2, system boundary

entries.title: Authentication today (magic link)
entries.answer: Users sign in with an email magic link — Auth.js passwordless login delivered by email — then a JWT session with organization membership and plan entitlements. Access is invite-based: we provision the organization and invite seats; users are not inventing their own unmanaged accounts into a tenant. Seat limits apply per plan.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Authentication; CUSTOMER_ACCESS.md

entries.title: SSO roadmap (honest)
entries.answer: Today authentication is email magic-link with org membership. Enterprise SSO — SAML/OIDC — is on the roadmap as an option for buyers that need it; we do not claim SSO is generally available today. For design partners we can discuss timeline honestly against your IdP requirements rather than overpromise.

entries.title: SOC 2 status (pursuing)
topics: do you have a SOC report
entries.answer: We are pursuing SOC 2 — readiness work is in progress — and we do not claim a completed SOC 2 certification or issued report today. Target path is Type I first, covering Security, Availability, and Confidentiality; Type II follows after an observation window. Until a report is issued, the honest language is 'pursuing' or 'in progress,' and we unblock IT with architecture, encryption, tenant isolation, no GL write-back, auth model, AI handling, DPA, and questionnaire answers.
entries.source: SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 §6 — never claim certified early

entries.title: SOC 2 scope path (sales-internal)
entries.answer: Internal: default Type I scope is Security + Availability + Confidentiality. Processing Integrity is deferred by default — do not market PI as third-party proof that ARR math or the engine is 'certified correct.' Privacy criterion skipped for now. Prefer sales unblockers (DPA, subprocessors, security one-pager, architecture) while controls and evidence mature. Never imply an issued report before it exists.

topics: what data goes to the AI
does Claude train on our data
keywords: what data goes to the ai
entries.answer: AI is used for narrative assistance — variance commentary and executive summary drafting — not to invent ledger numbers. Commentary is grounded in Financial Intelligence Engine outputs and governed report context. We minimize sending sensitive raw PII in prompts and prefer aggregated metrics. Treat the LLM provider as a subprocessor when prompts include customer-derived context; contractual training/retention posture follows the vendor terms we document for IT.

entries.answer: Anthropic is the primary narrative model with OpenAI as fallback. API keys reside on the server-side API only — not in static board HTML and not in the browser. That keeps model credentials out of client bundles and exported artifacts.

topics: how do you get our data
do we have to upload files
keywords: how do you get our data
entries.answer: For security-conscious and enterprise POCs we support a white-glove path: you grant read-only access — for example a Snowflake share, object-storage export, SFTP drop, or ERP export — and SMPL ops loads your tenant warehouse. No self-serve upload is required on that path. Access is documented, scoped, and revoked after the engagement or on request. We still do not write back to your GL or ERP.
entries.source: GO_LIVE_POC_DIRECT_DATA_ACCESS; IT Technical Diagram, Data Sources; SOC 2 §7.2

entries.title: White-glove vs self-serve onboarding
entries.answer: Two paths. White-glove direct access is available today for mid-market and enterprise POCs: read-only shares or exports, SMPL loads the warehouse, customer signs in with a magic link. Self-serve CSV upload and mapping is the scale path and continues to mature — first customers do not have to wait on self-serve. Typical implementation runs about four to six weeks once scope and data access are agreed.
entries.source: GO_LIVE_POC_DIRECT_DATA_ACCESS; GO_LIVE_POC_ONBOARDING; Technical Whitepaper timeline

entries.title: Role-based access
entries.answer: Access is role-based: finance can work at full GL-level drill-down, while executives and board viewers get summary-level, explained views. Org membership and plan entitlements gate what a signed-in user can reach inside the tenant.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Governance; IT Technical Diagram

entries.title: Secrets and API hardening
entries.answer: Production secrets live in environment/secret stores — not in git. The API uses a CORS allowlist, and internal keys protect billing/session sync paths between the app and API. AI provider keys stay on the API only. That is the hardening posture we describe for IT questionnaires.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Security Posture; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 §4.3

entries.answer: If someone asks about this meeting aide itself: it does not persist audio to disk. The rolling transcript stays in-memory in the browser tab for the session. entries.answer: We ingest from the systems finance already uses: ERP/GL such as NetSuite, Rillet, or QuickBooks; CRM such as Salesforce or HubSpot; billing such as Stripe or Maxio; HRIS such as Rippling or Workday; plus treasury extracts as needed. Today that is via versioned CSV or white-glove load — for example Snowflake share, object storage, or SFTP — normalized into our canonical model for reporting. Scheduled native connectors into that same model are on the roadmap; we do not claim they are generally available today.

entries.answer: Yes — we separate production and sandbox/staging environments for the app, API, and database so customer production data is not mixed with preview or staging work. That separation is part of how we describe change management and go-live hygiene to IT.

entries.title: Platform features overview
entries.answer: SMPL is a SaaS financial intelligence layer — not a BI dashboard and not an ERP. In the product you get executive dashboards, ARR/MRR waterfalls, the three financial statements with tie-outs, Actual vs Budget vs Forecast scenarios, pipeline and GTM views, board PowerPoint and MD&A-style Excel packages, and AI-assisted executive commentary grounded in the same numbers. Higher plans unlock Management P&L, workforce, and cash forecast modules. We sit above your GL, CRM, billing, and HR systems and do not post back to them.
entries.source: Architecture Master; Reporting Logic report catalog; GO_LIVE_GL3 plan entitlements; CFO Operating System UX

entries.title: ARR / MRR waterfall reporting
entries.answer: Yes — ARR and MRR are first-class. You get a roll-forward waterfall: beginning, new, expansion, contraction, churn, reactivation where modeled, and ending — with drilldown to the underlying movements. Retention concepts like NRR and GRR are part of the SaaS finance model, not bolt-on spreadsheet formulas. How you define ARR is configured for your org rather than forced into a generic template.
entries.source: Reporting Logic MRR/ARR; Technical Whitepaper native SaaS primitives; company context §3

entries.title: Three financial statements
topics: income statement balance sheet cash flow
entries.answer: Yes — income statement (P&L), balance sheet, and cash flow statement are core outputs, with validation so key tie-outs are checked as part of reporting — for example balance sheet balances and cash bridge to balance-sheet cash. Statement lines and waterfalls share one logic path with the dashboards and Excel packages, so you are not maintaining a separate export model.
entries.source: Reporting Logic financial statements + validation; Architecture Master

entries.title: Actual / Budget / Forecast scenarios
topics: do you support budget and forecast
entries.answer: Reporting is scenario-aware: Actual for closed periods, Budget for plan, Forecast for the rolling outlook, and a Combined view that uses Actual through the close month and Forecast thereafter. Close packages show variance columns — Actual vs Budget and Actual vs Forecast — so FP&A can review the same structure leadership already uses, not a one-scenario snapshot.
entries.source: Architecture Master scenario model; Reporting Logic Combined + period column layout

Two customers do not share one forced template; they share the same engine with different methodology configuration. Deep layout work happens at implementation, not as an ad-hoc drag-and-drop chart builder for every viewer.

Ongoing close is load → validate → finalize the period → generate executive packages — not rebuilding the model from scratch each month. Ad-hoc redesign of every chart by every user is not the product; durable methodology configuration for your org is. Timeline is designed around roughly four to six weeks once scope and data access are agreed.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper implementation; onboarding-paths KB; Close / reporting architecture (customer-safe wording)

entries.title: Management P&L and drilldown
topics: do you have a management P&L
can I drill into GL accounts
entries.answer: Management P&L with drilldown into the accounts behind a line — Actual vs Budget vs Forecast — is a core Professional-and-above capability. Starter focuses on executive, ARR, revenue, GTM, and pipeline surfaces; Management P&L is the natural expand module when FP&A wants statement-level operating review inside the app.
entries.source: Company context §3; GO_LIVE_GL3 management-pl entitlement; CFO Operating System section map

entries.title: Dashboards and exports share one logic
topics: is the board deck the same as the dashboard
one source of truth for exports
entries.answer: Dashboards and Excel/PowerPoint exports read the same service layer — one logic path, not a separate spreadsheet model maintained for the board deck. That is how we keep executive packages and the live app from drifting apart after close.
entries.source: Reporting Logic principles; Architecture Master API-first reporting

entries.title: GTM, pipeline, and cash views
entries.answer: Beyond core statements and ARR: Pipeline waterfall and opportunity views, GTM/marketing efficiency by channel, and — on Professional and above — cash forecast that respects SaaS billing timing rather than smoothing everything into GAAP revenue. Those modules sit in the same executive operating shell so finance and GTM are not living in disconnected tools.
entries.source: Reporting Logic waterfalls + marketing; company context §3; GO_LIVE_GL3 cash module

entries.title: Native connectors generally available (deflect)
topics: is the Salesforce connector live today
entries.answer: DEFLECT: do not claim self-serve native connectors are generally available. Say: "Today we land customers via versioned CSV or white-glove read-only loads into the same canonical model native connectors will use. I won't claim every named connector is GA — let's scope the data path that fits your IT and timeline."
